_note: Apex Utilities story spec, built from clients/apex-utilities/research.json per qiq-story-architect. One-sided, regulated-monopoly gas distribution utility — no supply-side fields present anywhere, per schema Step 1. REVISION (same day, 2026-09-15): the first draft of this spec assumed zero public reviews existed and dropped storyline slot 3 on that basis. Vansh then surfaced a Google share link that resolves to Apex's Google Business Profile — 2.5 stars, 52 reviews, missed entirely by the first research pass (it's a Search knowledge-panel listing, not a standalone review site). research.json and research.md have been corrected; this spec is revised to match. Slot 3 is back in (see storylines below), and slots 1/2 now lean on real, attributed review quotes rather than FAQ-structure inference. BOTH PRIOR OPEN ITEMS NOW RESOLVED: logo — Vansh supplied the real Apex Utilities Inc. logo PNG directly, saved to clients/apex-utilities/assets/logo.png, logoPath updated to match. Financial model framing — Vansh confirmed the cost-to-serve reframing over trying to quantify a fabricated 'brand reputation' dollar figure; see the financial block's own _note for the resolved methodology (churnUpliftPct is now solved backward from a real, computed avoidable-repeat-contact-cost figure, not a relabelled churn guess). CURRENCY DISPLAY (per Vansh, 2026-09-15): checked app/src/config/brand.js and app/src/utils/format.js directly — currency is currently just a literal symbol (NOUNS.currencySymbol) concatenated with the number, no ISO code or Intl currency formatting anywhere in the ~20 call sites that use it. A bare '$' would be visually indistinguishable from USD (every other client built so far - Rover, Kyndryl, Bed Bath & Beyond, Brooklinen - uses GBP/USD, so this hasn't come up before). Set brand.nouns.currencySymbol to 'CA$' (the standard disambiguation used by Canadian banks/retailers) instead of a bare '$', so every dollar figure in the app reads unambiguously as Canadian. Historical framing for context: FINANCIAL MODEL FRAMING (original problem statement): demandSideLtv is modelled as ~CA$1,080/year (average Alberta residential gas bill, derived from 2018 CER commodity/delivery breakdown data for ATCO Gas North/South adjusted for since-2018 inflation and carbon-levy increases — the most recent sourceable breakdown found; flagged as dated, not current-year billing data) times cohortHitWeekly=450 distinct customers/week newly hitting the dominant billing-dispute pattern, times churnUpliftPct=6. That churnUpliftPct number is a genuine modelling problem: Apex customers CANNOT switch distributor (confirmed in research — 'consumers cannot choose their distributor, it's determined by location'), so a literal 'at-risk of churning' framing is factually wrong for this client, unlike every prior client this pipeline has built (Rover, Kyndryl, Bed Bath & Beyond, Brooklinen all have real competitive churn). This is now a live financial narrative question, not a moot one — the Google reviews show real negative sentiment on exactly the categories (fees, policy rigidity) that would drive churn if switching were possible, so there's a genuine story to tell about reputational/regulatory risk even without churn in the literal sense. churnUpliftPct=6 should be read as a stand-in for 'relationship-quality erosion' (repeat-contact cost, complaint-escalation-to-AUC risk, reputational drag ahead of the next rate case), and the app's LTV-panel copy will need qiq-content-writer (or a manual copy pass) to say that explicitly rather than reusing Rover/Kyndryl's churn language verbatim — this is a review item, not resolved here. Contact volumes, driver splits, and per-contact CSAT/behaviour figures are modelled to be internally consistent with research.json, not real Apex operational data (Apex has not shared operational data with QiQ) — the Google review quotes are real, but weekly contact-centre volumes/CSAT numbers built around them are illustrative, same as every other client in this pipeline. Demo window set to the 5 weeks immediately following the real Aug 1, 2026 Phase 2 rate-class restructuring (3 Aug - 6 Sep 2026), since that regulatory change is now in effect as of today's research date (15 Sep 2026), not a future hypothetical. Palette/font are the template's default neutral palette, not Apex's real brand colours, matching the Kyndryl precedent (a QiQ demo is QiQ's product surface, not a reskin of the client's site).

client.name: Apex Utilities
client.industry: Regulated natural gas distribution utility (Alberta, Canada)

businessProfile.whatTheyDo: Apex Utilities distributes natural gas to roughly 82,000-85,000 residential, farm, and small-commercial customers across 90+ communities in Alberta, owning about 21,000 km of distribution pipeline out of 14 district offices headquartered in Leduc, AB.
businessProfile.revenueModel: Cost-of-service / performance-based (PBR) distribution rates set and approved by the Alberta Utilities Commission (AUC); customers pay a regulated distribution charge plus a pass-through gas commodity cost, with no price competition on the distribution side since Apex is the sole franchisee in its service territories.
businessProfile.cxRole: trust-and-safety-critical, not a brand differentiator — gas-emergency response, billing accuracy, and clear communication of AUC-approved rate changes carry real safety and regulatory stakes, but contact-centre quality cannot drive acquisition or retention since customers cannot choose their distributor.
businessProfile.marketPosition: One of Alberta's AUC-regulated gas distributors alongside ATCO Gas North and ATCO Gas South. Market share by customer count not publicly disclosed. Scope confirmed with Vansh as gas-only for this demo, despite one third-party source (Alberta's Utilities Consumer Advocate) also listing Apex among the province's regulated electricity distributors and default retailers.

competitors.name: ATCO Gas (North/South)
competitors.positioning: Much larger AUC-regulated gas distributor covering the rest of Alberta; not head-to-head, but the province's natural rate/service benchmark.

competitors.name: FortisAlberta / ENMAX Power / EPCOR
competitors.positioning: Regulated Alberta electricity distributors that set the province-wide bar for what an Albertan expects from 'their utility,' despite the different commodity.

competitors.name: Direct Energy / ATCO Energy / other competitive retailers
competitors.positioning: Compete for the retail commodity-supply contract layered on top of Apex's fixed distribution service; a customer can switch retailer but not distributor, so retailer confusion can still land as a misdirected call to Apex.

recentMoves.summary: Phase 2 rate restructuring took effect: Rate 1 redefined as under 4,000 GJ/year, Rate 2 (over 4,000 GJ) now mandatory for qualifying usage, irrigation accounts harmonized into Rate 1. Apex's FAQ spends 10 questions explaining it.

System Betterment Program completed confirmed pipe-replacement work in the Towns of High Level and Hanna and in Sturgeon County, with Apex's stated process being advance customer notices plus local-newspaper/social updates during the work.
AUC Decision 30302-D01-2025 set Apex's 2026 Annual PBR rate.

storylines.title: Billing and fee disputes escalate on top of an already-strained rate-change season

stats.shareNote: Rate Class / Bill Impact Questions (18.0%) and Billing & Fee Dispute Escalations (16.0%) are two standalone categories that combine to 34.0% of weekly volume — reported together here because research.json's Google reviews evidence shows they're the same underlying pattern (billing/fee disagreements that escalate into complaints about agent tone and policy rigidity), not because they're one category; see externally-evidenced quotes below.
stats.realEvidenceNote: Grounded in strong-confidence, directly quoted Google reviews (2.5-star profile, 52 reviews): a customer billed CA$3,143 in fees against CA$488 of actual gas use; a vacant-property customer charged a daily distribution fee for zero usage; multiple reviews independently describing phone agents as rude or unhelpful when these disputes come up. The Aug 1, 2026 Phase 2 rate restructuring is a real, dated trigger landing on top of an already-known-difficult category, not the storyline's sole basis.

storylines.title: An account falls through the billing cracks, then lands a CA$1,800 surprise

stats.shareNote: Only 3.0% of weekly volume (Missing Bill / Account Reconciliation Issues), but disproportionate CSAT damage when it happens — this taxonomy row has the lowest FCR (41%) and highest escalation rate (24%) of any driver.
stats.realEvidenceNote: Directly grounded in a real Google review: 8 months with no bill sent, service then cut off for 'non-payment,' followed by an unexplained CA$1,800 back-bill, with the customer questioning how a meter reading was even taken on an account the company said didn't exist. Rare, but the sharpest single CSAT collapse of any pattern found in research.

financial._note: REFRAMED (per Vansh, 2026-09-15): the app's computeLtvFinancials() formula (app/src/utils/ltvFinancial.js) is just cohortHitWeekly * (churnUpliftPct/100) * demandSideLtv * 52 - it doesn't care what churnUpliftPct means semantically, only qiq-content-writer's copy (data/ltvCopy.js) does. So instead of relabelling a fake churn number, churnUpliftPct is now solved backward from a real, directly-computed avoidable-cost figure: assume CA$6 per contact (blended BPO agent-time estimate - NOT a real Quantanite-supplied cost-per-contact figure, correct if Vansh has one) and 1 avoidable extra contact per affected customer. Annual avoidable repeat-contact cost = cohortHitWeekly(450) * 52 weeks * 1 contact * CA$6 = CA$140,400. churnUpliftPct = 140400 / (450*52*1080) * 100 = 0.56, chosen so the app's existing formula reproduces that CA$140,400 as its primary figure (total ~CA$171K once the panel's standard 1.22x secondary/tertiary weighting is applied). ACTION NEEDED AT STAGE 4 (qiq-content-writer): the LTV panel's label/copy must change from churn language ('Customer Churn Risk', 'at risk of leaving') to cost-to-serve language ('Avoidable Cost-to-Serve Exposure' or similar) - the number is now correct, the label is not, until that copy pass happens.

heroNarrativeDraft._note: Draft hero narrative arc for qiq-content-writer to render into content/executiveConstants.js HERO_CONTENT, following the Kyndryl precedent where the story spec itself carries no dedicated hero field but the draft is handed forward here.
heroNarrativeDraft.headline: The bill disputes were already a problem. The rate change just landed on top of them.
heroNarrativeDraft.paragraph1: Billing and fee disputes, including the wave of Rate Class / Bill Impact Questions triggered by the August 1 Phase 2 rate restructuring, are 34% of Apex's weekly contact volume combined, and independently evidenced on Apex's own public Google reviews: a 2.5-star profile with recurring complaints about disproportionate fees and rude phone handling, not a hypothesis. Most of these contacts start as a first call that resolves cleanly - first-contact CSAT is 4.3. The pattern breaks on the callback: continuation CSAT for the same customers drops to 2.3, and repeat-contact rate for this cohort has climbed from 17.5% to 22.6% over five weeks.
heroNarrativeDraft.paragraph2: Micro Coaching targeting clarity-of-communication and ownership on repeat contacts was applied from week 2; continuation CSAT begins recovering (2.0 in week 1 to 2.9 by week 5). Two things this doesn't fix: the rare but severe case of an account falling through the billing cracks entirely (one real customer went 8 months unbilled, then received an unexplained CA$1,800 back-bill), and the System Betterment construction-notification gap, a cross-team process issue between engineering scheduling and customer comms that behavioural coaching alone won't close. One genuine bright spot worth keeping in the story: Apex's field emergency-response team is already a strength, not a weakness - the same public reviews that complain about billing separately praise named technicians for fast, professional gas-leak response. The damage is concentrated in the phone/billing side of the house, not the field side.

methodology.financialSource: Assumed CA$6 cost per handled contact (a blended estimate, not an Apex figure) and one avoidable repeat contact per affected customer; affected customers per week are modelled
